thesis: Tbilisi in September thins out because the grapes decide when, and nobody treats the absence as unusual.
scene: It's just after seven and the marshrutka out of Ortachala is loading for Kakheti with more people than seats. Two of them are carrying empty plastic containers, which is the direction of travel that matters: empty going out, full coming back. A man in his fifties is on the phone establishing whether they will start Thursday or Friday, and the answer depends on somebody's uncle's opinion of the sugar. Nobody in this van is on holiday. They have taken the days because the harvest does not move, and the office already knows.

sceneAnchors.text: The station on the southern edge where the minibuses for Kakheti go from. In September the queue forms early and half of it is people with empty containers. Departures are frequent and unscheduled in the sense that they leave when full. The return traffic on Sunday nights is slower and heavier.

The market by the station, which in September fills with grapes sold by the crate rather than the kilo, and with the equipment for dealing with them. People buy in quantities that only make sense if you are making something. Nobody selling here is explaining what any of it is for.

The shared inner courtyards of the old town, where the returning containers end up and where a good deal of the city's wine is kept. In late September the courtyards smell of it. Balconies that were quiet in August have people on them again, and the conversation is about whose village had the better year.

locals: People take days off that were not planned in advance, because the date is set by the fruit and not by anyone's calendar. They go to the village their family comes from, which is a fact everybody knows about everybody, and they work — picking, carrying, pressing into vessels buried in the ground. The obligation is not framed as a holiday. Offices lose staff for a week in a rolling pattern through the month and absorb it without comment. What comes back to the city is containers, and a year's supply.

localWord.translation: the grape harvest, and the obligation to return for it
localWord.body: Not agricultural work so much as a claim your family's village has on you. The date is decided by the fruit. Everyone goes, and the city notices the gap.

changes: You stop seeing the city as the whole of the country. Everyone around you has somewhere else they are from and a week in September when they have to be there, and the city runs at reduced strength because of it. Tbilisi turns out to be a place a great many people are currently away from.
start: Asking people where they are from and getting a village rather than a district. You start noticing who is missing this week. If somebody asks you along you go, and you will be handed a crate within ten minutes of arriving because standing and watching is not one of the available positions. You come back with a container you did not bring.
stop: Expecting the month to hold still. Meetings move because somebody's harvest started early, and this is accepted as a reason in a way it would not be elsewhere. Tbilisi in September is arranged around an event that will not negotiate its date, and the city has agreed to be the flexible party.
returns: A sense of where things come from, which most cities have successfully hidden. The wine on the table in October was carried back on a minibus by somebody at the table, from a village they will name if you ask. Nothing about that supply chain is abstract, and September is the month you can watch it happen.
remember: Everyone here is from somewhere smaller, and in September they go.

items.label: July
items.body: The heat empties the city toward the mountains, for relief not work.

items.label: September
items.body: The city thins because the harvest called, and returns carrying wine.

items.label: December
items.body: Everyone is back and the year's wine is on every table.
